note: Curated by hand. Entries marked manuallyVerified:false must be opened and checked before submission. None of these sources is proof of the SpeakingTree article's claims.

items.title: Meditation and Mindfulness: What You Need To Know
items.organisation: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), US National Institutes of Health
items.investigated: A plain-language summary of what is known about meditation and mindfulness, how they are practised, and what is understood about their safety.
items.relevance: A balanced starting point on attention and mindfulness practice, written for the general public.
items.caution: A general overview. It does not evaluate the article's specific ideas.

items.title: Mindfulness
items.investigated: Practical public guidance on mindfulness and how paying attention to the present moment relates to mental wellbeing.
items.relevance: Describes noticing thoughts and feelings as a way of understanding yourself, which parallels the article's self-awareness theme.
items.caution: Public guidance, not a research study. It suggests speaking to a professional if you are struggling.

items.title: Mindfulness
items.investigated: A psychology resource hub on mindfulness, including how it is defined and how it is used in stress management.
items.relevance: Connects thought observation and acceptance to how psychologists describe mindfulness.
items.caution: A topic hub. Individual linked pages vary in the strength of their evidence.

items.title: Meditation Programs for Psychological Stress and Well-being: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.investigated: Reviewed 47 randomised clinical trials of meditation programmes across a range of mental and physical health outcomes.
items.relevance: Shows how researchers test whether mindfulness-style programmes change outcomes such as anxiety, depression and stress.
items.caution: Reviewed structured programmes, not the article's philosophy, and effects varied by outcome. It does not show meditation is better than other active treatments.

items.title: Mindfulness-based therapy: A comprehensive meta-analysis
items.investigated: A meta-analysis of studies of mindfulness-based therapies for a range of psychological problems.
items.relevance: Looks at therapy programmes that teach people to observe thoughts and feelings with acceptance.
items.caution: Covers clinical therapy programmes delivered by trained professionals, which is different from a short self-guided exercise.

items.topic: Why fighting a thought can backfire
items.title: Paradoxical effects of thought suppression
items.organisation: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
items.investigated: A laboratory study in which people were asked to deliberately not think about a specific thing, and how often the thought returned.
items.relevance: Related to the idea that pushing a thought away can keep it in mind, which fits the article's point about not fighting every thought.
items.caution: A small laboratory study of thought suppression. It was not a study of meditation and does not prove the article's claims.
